title: Dijkstra
sub: BFS with weights: a heap, lazy deletion instead of decrease-key, 0-1 BFS, Bellman–Ford and garbage-free Dijkstra in Unity
cards/0/body:
Network Delay Time (LeetCode #743). A network of n nodes numbered 1..n, times[i] = [u, v, w]: a signal travels from u to v in w (the edge is directed). A signal is sent from node k. How long until every node has received it? If some node never gets it, return −1. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 100, up to 6000 edges, 0 ≤ w ≤ 100.

The answer is the largest of the shortest distances from k: the signal runs along every edge at once, and the farthest node hears it last. So we need shortest distances from k to everyone. The signals for Dijkstra:

1. A shortest path — the minimum sum of weights — from a single source.
2. Edge weights differ: BFS counts edges, not time.
3. Weights are non-negative: time, distance, price.

In a game: a tile map where road costs 1, sand 2 and swamp 5 — the cheapest path for a unit; "how many seconds the AI needs to reach each point"; fire spreading through rooms.
cards/0/code:
// 1→2 in 4, 1→3 in 1, 3→2 in 2, 2→3 in 1, 2→4 in 1, 3→4 in 5, 3→5 in 7, 4→5 in 3
int t = NetworkDelayTime(times, n: 5, k: 1);   // 7: node 5 is the farthest, path 1→3→2→4→5
cards/1/q: Where do you need Dijkstra because plain BFS is not enough? Select all that apply.
cards/1/options/0: A unit on a tile map: road costs 1, sand 2, swamp 5 — find the cheapest path
cards/1/options/1: How many seconds until fire reaches each room, when doors burn through in different times
cards/1/options/2: The fewest knight moves from one square of a board to another
cards/1/options/3: How many rooms of a maze are reachable from the entrance
cards/1/options/4: The shortest route between cities, with roads of different lengths in kilometres
cards/1/explain: Sand and swamp, doors and kilometres are different non-negative weights with a minimum sum: that is Dijkstra. Every knight move costs the same — one move — so BFS by levels gives the shortest path in moves. Reachability is not about length at all: any traversal will do.
cards/2/title: Why BFS breaks, and the brute-force version
cards/2/body:
In BFS a queue level is a number of edges, and the first touch of a node is final. With weights that is wrong: the edge 1→2 costs 4, but the path 1→3→2 costs 1 + 2 = 3. BFS would set dist[2] = 4 and never touch it again.

Dijkstra's greedy idea. Among the nodes whose distance is not final yet, take the node u with the smallest estimate dist[u]. It is already final: any other path to u leaves the final region through some non-final node whose dist is no smaller, and weights ≥ 0 only add to it. Mark u final and relax its edges: dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w).

Naively that minimum is found by scanning: V steps, each a pass over all V nodes. Time O(V² + E). With n = 100 that is 10⁴ operations — fine. But on a game map a node is a cell.
cards/3/q: A 256×256 map with cells of different cost, moves in 4 directions. How many operations does Dijkstra with a scan for the minimum take per search, and what follows?
cards/3/options/0: ≈ 4.3·10⁹ — tens of seconds; the minimum has to come out faster than a scan
cards/3/options/1: ≈ 2.6·10⁵ — about the number of edges, it fits in a frame
cards/3/explain: There are V = 65,536 cells, and each of the V steps scans all V: V² ≈ 4.3·10⁹. At the rule of thumb of 10⁸ simple operations per second that is about 40 seconds for one path. There are only about 4V ≈ 2.6·10⁵ edges: the bottleneck is not them but finding the minimum. That is what a heap replaces.
cards/3/wrong/1: 2.6·10⁵ is the edges, and relaxing them really is cheap. But before every step the scan looks for the minimum among all 65,536 cells.
cards/3/wrong/2: Each cell becomes final once — but to pick it, the scan walks all V cells every time.
cards/4/title: The idea: a heap and lazy deletion
cards/4/body:
A min-heap gives the minimum (the lesson on .NET collections and the unit on heaps): "distance, node" pairs, Enqueue and Dequeue in O(log). The catch: when dist[v] improves, v's old entry is already in the heap, PriorityQueue cannot change a priority (decrease-key), and finding an entry in a heap is O(n).

Lazy deletion. Push v again with the new distance. The new entry is smaller and comes out first. When the old one comes out later, its d is greater than dist[v] — the entry is stale, so skip it.

Invariant: if the heap yields (d, u) and d == dist[u], then dist[u] is final — the heap gives the minimum, and weights are ≥ 0.

Cost. Every successful relaxation adds an entry, so there are at most E of them, and each heap operation is O(log E) = O(log V), since E ≤ V². In total O((V + E) log V). On a 256×256 map: about 2.6·10⁵ entries × 18 ≈ 5·10⁶ — by the same rule of thumb, tens of milliseconds instead of 40 seconds.
cards/4/flow/3: yes → dist[v] = d + w, push (dist[v], v)
cards/5/explain: An entry with d greater than dist[u] was pushed before an improvement — skip it. Relax when the path through u is strictly shorter; the condition "dist[v] is still ∞" is a BFS habit, and with weights it breaks the answer. Push the whole new distance to v, not the edge weight. If any node is left at ∞, the signal never reached it: the answer is −1.
cards/6/task: Step through Dijkstra on the example: 5 nodes, the signal starts at node 1. The queue holds "distance:node" pairs. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does with an improved node and with a stale entry.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: dist[2] = 3 and Enqueue(2, 3); the entry 4:2 stays in the queue
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Find 4:2 in the queue and replace it with 3:2
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: node 2 is already queued, it is not pushed twice
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: We popped 1:3. Edge 3→2 has weight 2: 1 + 2 = 3, while dist[2] = 4 and 4:2 is already queued. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: You cannot change a priority inside PriorityQueue, and searching a heap for an entry is O(n). So we push a new entry 3:2: it comes out earlier, because 3 < 4. The old 4:2 stays behind as garbage and is filtered out when it surfaces.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: 4:2 comes out of the queue, but dist[2] is already 3 — node 2 is final and its edges have been checked. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: d = 4 > dist[2] = 3: the entry was pushed before the improvement — this is lazy deletion. Without the check the answer would still be right — relaxing with a larger d improves nothing — but the node's edges would be walked again, and on a dense graph that is a lot of wasted checks.
cards/7/q: On the example from the rig this code returns 8 instead of 7. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: This is the BFS habit: "whoever touches a node first is right". Node 2 got 4 over the direct edge from 1, and the path 1→3→2 costing 3 changes nothing — so node 5 keeps 8 over the edge 3→5 instead of 7 through 4. The condition must be d + w < dist[v]: a node may be improved any number of times, and only leaving the heap makes it final.
cards/8/body:
The invariant "popped means final" rests on detours through other nodes only adding cost. A negative edge breaks it: 1→2 costs 2, 2→4 costs 1, 1→3 costs 5, 3→2 costs −4. Dijkstra pops node 2 at distance 2, treats it as final and relaxes its edge: dist[4] = 3. Yet the path 1→3→2 costs 1, so node 4 is really at 2. The scanning version from the start of the lesson never expands node 2 again, and 4 stays at 3. The lazy heap version pushes 2 again and expands it a second time — the answer survives, but "popped means final" no longer holds: nodes leave the heap many times, and on unlucky graphs the number of repeats grows exponentially.

Bellman–Ford does not pick a minimum; it relaxes every edge V − 1 times. A shortest path without cycles has at most V − 1 edges, and after pass i, dist[v] is at most the cost of the best path to v with at most i edges. Time O(V·E). If pass V still improves something, a negative-weight cycle is reachable from the source, and no shortest path exists.

Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (LeetCode #787): n ≤ 100 cities, flights with prices, find the cheapest way from src to dst with at most k stops. Prices are positive, but Dijkstra on its own does not respect a limit on the number of edges. At most k stops means at most k + 1 flights: exactly k + 1 passes of Bellman–Ford. Each pass reads the previous pass's array and writes into a copy — otherwise one pass could chain several flights in a row.

In games negative weights barely exist: a bonus tile is made cheaper but not negative — and Dijkstra still holds.
cards/9/body:
A common special case: a step costs 0 or 1. "The fewest walls to break to get through": entering an empty cell costs 0, a wall costs 1. "Ladders and teleports are free, a step costs 1". Minimum Cost to Make at Least One Valid Path in a Grid (#1368): following a cell's arrow costs 0, changing its direction costs 1.

No heap is needed here. Take a deque: if the edge costs 0, the neighbour goes to the front; if 1, to the back. The deque then holds distances of just two values, d and d + 1, in order — so the minimum always comes out first, like from a heap, but in O(1). Time O(V + E).

.NET has no deque of its own (the unit on windows and deques): here it is LinkedList<T> — the simplest choice, but every list node is a heap object. On a hot path, use your own ring buffer over an array.
cards/10/q: A 100×100 grid with an arrow in every cell. A step along the arrow is free, a step in any other direction costs 1. You need the cheapest path from corner to corner. What do you use?
cards/10/options/0: 0-1 BFS: a deque, 0-edges to the front, 1-edges to the back
cards/10/options/1: Plain BFS with a queue: the weights are only 0 and 1 anyway
cards/10/explain: Weights of only 0 and 1 are the signal for 0-1 BFS: O(V + E), about 5·10⁴ operations. Dijkstra with a heap is correct too, but pays an extra log on every operation.
cards/10/wrong/1: BFS counts edges: to it a free step is a level like any paid one. Zero-weight edges break "level = distance".
cards/10/wrong/2: Bellman–Ford is correct but O(V·E): 10⁴ cells × 4·10⁴ edges = 4·10⁸ — seconds where one linear pass is enough.
cards/11/title: Unity: Dijkstra without PriorityQueue and without garbage
cards/11/body:
Unity has no PriorityQueue, so take your own heap from the unit on heaps. What else sets the game version apart from a LeetCode solution:

1. The key is one long. The distance goes in the high 32 bits, the cell in the low ones: ((long)d << 32) | (uint)cell. With d ≥ 0, the order of the long is the order by distance. The heap compares numbers — no tuples, no comparer.
2. A grid needs no adjacency lists. The neighbours of cell i are i ± 1 and i ± w with edge checks: no memory for edges.
3. The cost lives on the cell. The map stores the cost of entering a cell (0 is a wall), not the weight of every edge.
4. Arrays live in fields. dist and the heap are allocated once; with lazy deletion the heap holds at most E + 1 entries, 4V + 1 on a 4-neighbour grid (with the cost on the cell it is in fact at most V — the flow field lesson shows why).

If a search is long, it is sliced across frames: N heap pops per frame, with the state kept in fields.
cards/11/deep:
Why the greedy step is right. Let u be the first node popped with a wrong distance, and P a true shortest path to u. P leaves the set of final nodes into some node y; y's predecessor on P is final, so its edges were relaxed and dist[y] is correct. Weights are ≥ 0, so dist[y] ≤ len(P) < dist[u] — and the heap would have yielded y before u. A contradiction. With a negative weight, the "≤ len(P)" step is exactly what collapses.

The exact cost. With lazy deletion the heap holds up to E entries: O(E log E) = O(E log V). An indexed heap with decrease-key (an array "node → position in the heap") keeps at most V entries, but the complexity is the same, O((V + E) log V), and there is more code. A Fibonacci heap gives O(E + V log V) in theory and is slower than a binary heap in practice because of constants and cache misses. For a dense graph (E ≈ V²) the best option is the scan from the start of the lesson, O(V²): a heap does not pay for itself there.

Small integer weights. Cell costs of 1–9 call for a bucket queue (Dijkstra with buckets, Dial's algorithm): an array of lists indexed by distance, with a pointer that only moves forward. O(E + V·C), where C is the largest weight, with no log and no comparisons. 0-1 BFS is its special case with C = 1.

Jobs and Burst. A single Dijkstra search is sequential: one heap per search, and each step depends on the previous one. What you parallelise is not a search but searches: each agent or each goal gets its own IJob with its own NativeArrays for dist and the heap. The arrays are allocated with Allocator.Persistent and reused across frames; Burst keeps managed objects out of a job, so the heap is your own, over a NativeArray<long>.
cards/12/q: You are solving Network Delay Time out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: edges are directed, weights are non-negative, what to return if someone is missed
cards/12/items/1: Reduce the problem: the answer is the largest shortest distance from k
cards/12/items/2: Say why not BFS: weights differ, so the first touch is not final
cards/12/items/3: Idea: Dijkstra with a heap, skip stale entries when they come out
cards/12/items/4: Code with the invariant: a popped node with d == dist[u] is final
cards/12/items/5: Run the example: 1→2 at 4 improves to 3 through node 3
cards/12/items/6: Complexity O((V + E) log V) and edge cases: an unreachable node, a zero-weight edge
cards/12/explain: First the problem and the reduction to shortest paths, then why the familiar BFS does not fit: that shows the interviewer the choice of Dijkstra is deliberate. The example with the 4 → 3 improvement shows lazy deletion at work. Edge cases come last: −1 for an unreachable node, and zero weights, on which Dijkstra is still correct.
